title: Midunu Groundnut Soup
author: Selassie Atadika
desc: A chef's meatless version — a cup and a half of groundnut paste into eight cups of stock, and a warning about what happens if you stop before the oil separates.
longDesc: This is a Ghanaian chef's groundnut soup and it is built the other way round from the household versions: no meat at all, just groundnut paste and tomato paste bloomed with cayenne, slowly let down with two cups of stock and cooked covered for twenty minutes, then the remaining six cups stirred in. Ginger, onion, optional mushroom powder and salt follow, and it boils thirty to forty minutes until the oil separates and is released from the groundnut paste. Blanched or sautéed vegetables go in at the end. Her warning about under-cooking it is the most useful sentence written about this dish.
ingredients: 375 ml (1 1/2 cups) smooth natural peanut butter or groundnut paste
7.5-15 ml (1/2-1 tbsp) ground cayenne pepper, to taste
Blanched or sautéed vegetables of choice — green beans, eggplant, carrots, okra and/or cauliflower
steps: Mix the peanut butter and tomato paste with the cayenne pepper in a pot and slowly blend in 2 cups of the stock.
Cook on medium heat, covered, stirring occasionally, for 20 minutes.
Add the remaining 6 cups of stock, stirring it in slowly.
Add the ginger, the mushroom powder if using, the onion and the salt.
Boil 30 to 40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the oil separates and is released from the groundnut paste.
Add the blanched or sautéed vegetables and the chilli and cook a few minutes more.
Serve, or reduce it further to use as a sauce.
chefTips: Her warning is the single most useful thing in the groundnut soup literature: if you do not let the soup cook until the oil separates, it can cause discomfort during digestion. The endpoint is not cosmetic.
Two cups of stock first, blended in slowly, then the other six. Adding all eight at once leaves you with lumps of undissolved paste.
Covered for the first twenty minutes, uncovered for the thirty to forty. The lid comes off when the long reduction starts.
A cup and a half of paste to eight cups of stock is a soup, not a stew — this is thinner than the diaspora versions and it is meant to be.
Vegetables are blanched or sautéed SEPARATELY and stirred in at the end, so they keep their colour and bite. It is a chef's touch and it works.
Mushroom powder is her optional umami rather than a traditional ingredient, and it stands in neatly for the dried fish or shrimp a household cook would use.
Reduce it down further and it becomes a sauce — her own note, and a good way to use leftovers.
commonMistakes: Stopping before the oil separates, which her source explicitly warns causes digestive discomfort.
All eight cups of stock at once.
Cooking the vegetables in the soup rather than separately.
Leaving the lid on for the whole cook.
Expecting the thickness of a diaspora groundnut stew.
sources: Adapted from a recipe published with 'Game-changing chef Selassie Atadika is bringing Africa's bounty to the table', Sunday Times (South Africa), 9 August 2020. BYLINE CAUTION: one fetch returned the byline 'Selassie Atadika' and a second returned only the date line with no person named, so THE BYLINE IS UNVERIFIED. The article profiles Atadika — the Ghanaian chef behind Midunu in Accra — and presents the recipe as hers. Yield as printed: 'Serves: 6'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 375ml (1½ cups) smooth natural peanut butter or groundnut paste; 60ml (¼ cup) tomato paste; 7.5ml — 15ml (½ tbsp- 1 tbsp) ground cayenne pepper, to taste; 2 litres (8 cups) stock; 5ml (1 tsp) fresh ginger, grated; 15ml (1 tbsp) mushroom powder, optional; 60ml (¼ cup) finely minced onion; 10ml (2 tsp) salt; blanched or sautéed vegetables of choice — green beans, eggplant, carrots, okra and/or cauliflower; chilli. NOTE: the first fetch listed metric only; the cup equivalents came from the second fetch.

Method verbatim: (1) 'Mix the peanut butter and tomato paste with cayenne pepper in a pot and slowly blend in 2 cups stock. Cook on medium heat, covered, and stir occasionally for 20 minutes.' (2) 'Add remaining 6 cups stock, stirring in slowly. Reduce heat to medium-low.' (3) 'Add ginger, mushroom powder, if using, onion and salt.' (4) 'Boil for 30-40 minutes, stirring occasionally until the oil separates and is released from the groundnut paste.' (5) Add vegetables and chilli and cook a few minutes.

THE WARNING, verbatim, and the reason the oil-separation endpoint across this whole dish family should be taken seriously: 'If you don't let the soup cook until the oil separates, it can cause discomfort during digestion.' No other source consulted explains WHY the endpoint matters; this one does.
ALSO FROM THE AUTHOR, verbatim: 'The soup can be reduced down a bit further and used as a sauce.'

THIS IS THE ONLY MEATLESS DOCUMENTED GROUNDNUT SOUP, and it is vegetarian as written provided the stock is. Its mushroom powder is a chef's substitution for the dried fish or shrimp umami a household version would carry.
PEANUT RATIO POSITION: 375 ml of paste to 2 litres of stock is the thinnest documented concentration relative to liquid. For the full fivefold spread across six sources see the sources at GHA013.
ON THE CHEF: Atadika runs Midunu in Accra and is one of the few internationally recognised Ghanaian chefs whose recipes are retrievable in print. Her garifoto is published at GHA055.
reheating: Gentle heat with stock or water. Add fresh vegetables rather than reheating the originals.
healthBenefits: Vegetarian as written with a vegetable stock.
Groundnut paste supplies plant protein, niacin, folate and vitamin E.
The separately cooked vegetables retain far more vitamin C than ones boiled in the soup.
Lower in fat per serving than the meat-based versions.
culturalNote: A Ghanaian chef writing down her groundnut soup with metric measures, a stated endpoint and a physiological reason for it is exactly what the rest of this dish's documentation lacks. That the soup is meatless is also worth noting: groundnut soup is often assumed to need meat, and one of the country's best-known chefs publishes it without any.
